common_name 'Hybrid Zinnia' is this catalog's own disambiguating label and appears on no admissible page. NC State's dedicated page gives only 'Zinnia' (Common Name(s) field, <title> parenthetical, description opener; its common-name page is titled 'Zinnia - Zinnia marylandica'), which cannot be used because it is the genus name and collapses into Common Zinnia (Zinnia elegans). Searched at landing for any other name rendered for this exact taxon: RHS has only cultivar and series pages (Zahara Series, Double Zahara Fire, 'Pas553645' and others; the Zahara Series page gives Name Status Unresolved and no common name), and a series name names a cultivar group, not the hybrid; UF/IFAS FPS-623 is a genus-level Zinnia spp. sheet (Common name(s): zinnia); Clemson HGIC's zinnia factsheet is multi-species and refers to the taxon only through the Zahara series; no UMD, Penn State or UGA page was found; MoBot refuses this machine and its search surfaces only a cultivar page. The owner should decide whether to keep this coined label.

The hybrid sign could not be confirmed: NC State renders 'Zinnia marylandica' without a multiplication sign; RHS has no species-level page (its cultivar pages also write 'Zinnia marylandica'), and MoBot was not readable.

records.name_note: NC State's page-title parenthetical lists eight alphabetized common names, including Trailing Lantana, and NC State's page description calls the plant Trailing lantana. RHS's page title is 'Lantana montevidensis | trailing lantana', and its 'Other common names' lists trailing lantana, weeping lantana. NC State lists Camara montevidensis, Lantana sellowiana and Lippia montevidensis as 'Previously known as'; RHS lists Lantana sellowiana as a synonym and gives Name Status Correct.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State (species page): 'This plant is toxic to humans, dogs, cats, and horses if ingested. The leaves and sap are skin irritants. Wear protective clothing and gloves when handling this plant.' Its summary line says 'This plant has medium severity poison characteristics' and the Poisonous to Humans block (human-scoped) gives Poison Severity: Medium; Poison Symptoms: Vomiting, diarrhea, dilated pupils, labored respiration; the leaves may cause dermatitis.; Poison Toxic Principle: Pentacyclic triterpenoids; Causes Contact Dermatitis: Yes; Poison Part (complete): Fruits, Leaves, Sap/Juice, Seeds, Stems. Its separate Problems field lists Contact Dermatitis, Poisonous to Humans, Problem for Cats, Problem for Children, Problem for Dogs, Problem for Horses. NC State Edibility field: 'Toxic if ingested.' NC State Plant Type field: Annual, Ground Cover, Perennial, Shrub. RHS: 'Harmful if eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling' and 'Pets (dogs, rabbits, rodents): Harmful if eaten.' The sources do not disagree on scope (neither restricts the hazard to fruit only).

records.name_note: NC State's dedicated Ipomoea tricolor page has a bare-binomial H1. Its <title> parenthetical and its stacked Common Name(s) list give the same five names in the same alphabetical order: Flying Saucers, Grannyvine, Heavenly Blue Morning Glory, Morning Glory, Pearly Gates Morning Glory. The description prose opens with 'the morning glory'. That name collides with the already-landed Common Morning Glory (Ipomoea purpurea), so this record lands under the list's first item, Flying Saucers. The page's 'Previously known as' field names Convolvulus venustus.
records.toxicity_detail: Source: NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox page for Ipomoea tricolor. Page prose (Description section): "This plant is toxic to dogs, cats, and horses. Ingestion of the seeds of this plant can cause hallucinations. It is also recommended to wear protective gloves when handling the morning glory." The page's Problems list carries Poisonous to Humans, Problem for Cats, Problem for Dogs, Problem for Horses and Weedy, and its tags include #poisonous, #problem for dogs, #problem for horses and #problem for cats. Plant Type lists Annual, Poisonous and Vine. The 'Poisonous to Humans' block is human-scoped (the Problem for Cats/Dogs/Horses tags and the prose sentence above are separate from it): Poison Severity: Low. Poison Symptoms: "Ingestion of the seeds can cause hallucinations, dilated pupils, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and drowsiness. numbness of extremities, and muscle tightness. Ingestion of the leaves and stems may cause vomiting." Poison Toxic Principle: "Contains lysergic acids that causes hallucinations much like LSD". Causes Contact Dermatitis: No. Poison Part: Seeds. Fruit Description: "The small, black seeds are poisonous." The page does not give a pet-specific symptom list, dose or poison part for cats or dogs. Source disagreement within the page: the Poison Part field lists only Seeds while the Poison Symptoms text also describes vomiting from leaves and stems, and the prose recommends protective gloves for handling although the block says Causes Contact Dermatitis: No.
unknowns: is_houseplant is false (set at landing): NC State describes an outdoor annual vine (Life Cycle: Annual), its Landscape Location field lists Container, Hanging Baskets and Patio with no Houseplants value, and no admissible source addresses indoor culture.

No admissible page other than NC State was found for this exact taxon: the Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder search for 'ipomoea tricolor' returned no results, and direct RHS URLs for Ipomoea tricolor returned 404; no dedicated page was found at Clemson HGIC, UF/IFAS, Penn State, UMD or UGA. All fields therefore rest on the single NC State page.

'Morning Glory', the prose opener, collides with the landed Common Morning Glory (Ipomoea purpurea), so the record lands under the first Common Name(s) list item, Flying Saucers. It was researched as Heavenly Blue Morning Glory, the list's third entry, which also echoes the page's cultivar 'Heavenly Blue'.

toxicity scope: NC State's human-scoped Poison block lists Poison Part: Seeds, Low severity, Contact Dermatitis No; but its prose says the plant is toxic to dogs, cats and horses without naming a part, and recommends gloves for handling. The Poison Symptoms text also mentions vomiting from leaves and stems. No cat- or dog-specific symptoms, dose or part is given.
is_edible false rests on NC State stating the seeds are poisonous and that ingesting the leaves and stems may cause vomiting; no source addresses use as food.
soil_ph_min/soil_ph_max null: NC State lists Acid (<6.0), Alkaline (>8.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0) together, so open-ended bands give no floor or ceiling.
water_regime null: NC State gives only 'moist, well-drained soil' (a soil adjective, not a watering instruction) and 'does not tolerate standing water'; no watering statement or interval.
fertilize_strength/fertilize_interval_days null: NC State says it 'will perform well in poor soil with little or no fertilizer' with no dilution or schedule.
direct_sun_hours_max null: the only hour figure on the page is the site-wide Light legend ('6 or more hours'), which is a minimum, not a species ceiling.

mature_height_in 96-120 and mature_spread_in 36-72 come from NC State's Dimensions block (8 ft 0 in - 10 ft 0 in; 3 ft 0 in - 6 ft 0 in), converted to inches; this is a twining vine that 'will require support', so the height may reflect a support-climbing habit.
soil_base garden_bed is inferred from NC State planting guidance (soil texture Loam (Silt) and Sand; also usable in containers and hanging baskets); the page gives no potting mix.
Temperature, humidity, light in foot-candles, chill damage and water interval fields: no admissible source states them.

RHS's subtitle and MoBot's single "Common Name" line both give "everlasting flower"; NC State's page title parenthetical and its alphabetized Common Name(s) list run Everlasting Daisy, Everlasting Flower, Everlasting Gold, Paper Daisy, Strawflower (so Everlasting Flower is in it, but not first). "Strawflower" is the name MoBot's Noteworthy Characteristics prose uses ("commonly called strawflower"), NC State's description opens with "Strawflower" and calls it "the common name strawflower", and RHS lists it under "Other common names". The name is therefore recorded as Everlasting Flower, led by RHS and MoBot, with strawflower as the widely used alternative.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets, toxicity_detail and is_edible are null: the NC State page for this exact taxon carries no Poison block, no Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tags and no edibility statement, and MoBot and RHS do not address toxicity or eating. No admissible source was found that names this plant (or Helichrysum bracteatum) for cats or dogs.

is_houseplant is false (set at landing): no admissible source frames this as a houseplant. NC State, MoBot and RHS treat it as an outdoor annual or short-lived tender perennial for beds, borders, containers and cutting gardens.

NC State's structured Light field also lists 'Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours)', but MoBot's structured Sun field and RHS's Position field list full sun only. direct_sun_hours_max is null: no species-specific prose gives an hour figure. NC State's '6 or more hours' is the site-wide light-category legend text.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max are null: NC State ticks Acid (<6.0), Alkaline (>8.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0), which are open-ended bands, and RHS lists 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral' in Growing Conditions. Its Cultivation line says neutral to alkaline, and MoBot gives no pH. Sources disagree on a range, so no bound is set.

soil_drainage is moderate on NC State's Good Drainage plus Moist (Occasionally Dry) tags and RHS's moist but well-drained. MoBot says 'dry to medium, well-drained' and NC State's description says 'average to dry soils' with moderate drought tolerance. This is not fast drainage, but sources lean drier than RHS.

water_regime is dry_surface_between from MoBot's structured Water field 'Dry to medium'. It conflicts mildly with RHS's soil moisture 'Moist but well-drained' and NC State's Moist/Occasionally Dry tags, and NC State's drought-tolerance remark is a trait, not a watering instruction. water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est and water_estimate_basis are null because the plant is an in-ground annual and no source frames watering as an interval or dry-down.

Humidity, indoor day/night temperature, chill_damage_f, cool_rest_note and light_fc fields are null: no admissible source gives these. MoBot's and NC State's USDA zone ranges (8-10) are growing-range figures, not a damage-onset temperature, and RHS's hardiness rating H2 is likewise not used for chill_damage_f.

Size differs by source. NC State and MoBot give 1-5 ft tall and 6-18 in wide (used here). RHS gives Max Height 0.5-1 metres (about 20-39 in) and Max Spread 0.1-0.5 metres (about 4-20 in) on a profile describing it as an upright annual. MoBot says species plants may reach 5 ft while popular cultivars typically grow 2-3 ft, with some 12 in dwarfs; NC State says some cultivars reach up to 5 feet, most are 2-3 feet, with some 12-inch dwarf varieties.

Signet Marigold is a listed alternate name, not the lead name. NC State also shows a 'Previously known as:' entry of Tagetes erecta on this page; this record does not adopt or borrow from that name.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State (Tagetes tenuifolia page): a page-top banner reads 'This plant has low severity poison characteristics.' and points 'See below' to the block headed 'Poisonous to Humans:', which is human-scoped (this severity rating comes from that Poisonous to Humans heading, not from any cat/dog tag): Poison Severity: Low. Poison Symptoms: Skin irritation is minor, or typically only lasting a few minutes. Poison Toxic Principle: Phototoxic thiophene derivatives. Causes Contact Dermatitis: Yes. Poison Part: Flowers, Roots, Sap/Juice. Plant Type tags: Annual, Herbaceous Perennial, Poisonous (three values). The page carries no Problem-for-Cats or Problem-for-Dogs tag. Edibility (same page, exact condition): 'The flowers of some cultivars have a pleasant citrus-like flavour and can be used sparingly as a flavouring or as a garnish.' Note that Flowers are also listed as a Poison Part for contact dermatitis, so the edible use is conditional (some cultivars only, flowers only, used sparingly) and the sap/flowers/roots can irritate skin. Only NC State was available among admissible sources.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets left null: NC State's poison data is human-scoped (Poisonous to Humans block) with no Problem-for-Cats or Problem-for-Dogs tag on the page, and no other admissible page for this exact taxon could be read.

is_edible is true but conditional: NC State's Edibility field says the flowers of some cultivars have a pleasant citrus-like flavour and can be used sparingly as a flavouring or as a garnish; the same page lists Flowers, Roots and Sap/Juice as Poison Parts for contact dermatitis (low severity, phototoxic thiophene derivatives). Not all cultivars are described as flavourful.
